Surah al-Fajr (The Dawn)

Meccan, and its verses are thirty.

﴿By the dawn.﴾ God, glory be to Him, swears by the dawn, just as He swore by the morning when He said: ﴿And by the morning when it brightens.﴾ It is also said that what is meant by it is the dawn prayer (salat al-fajr).

﴿And by ten nights﴾. These are the ten days of Dhu al-Hijja. For this reason, the dawn (al-fajr) has been interpreted as the dawn of ʿArafa or the dawn of al-Nahr (the day of sacrifice), or as the last ten nights of Ramadan. Their indefiniteness (tankir) is for glorification (li-l-tafkhim, emphasis and magnification). It is also read as "وَلَيالٍ عَشْرٍ" with the genitive construction (idafa, grammatical annexation), so that "ʿashr" refers to the days.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 89, verse 3:

﴿By the even and the odd﴾. That is: all things, their even and their odd; or the even and odd of these nights. It has been narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) explained them as the Day of Sacrifice (yawm al-nahr) and the Day of 'Arafah. Many opinions have been reported concerning them, and Allah Most High knows the reality of the matter best. It has also been read with a kasra on the waw (al-witr), and both are two dialects, like al-habr and al-hibr (ink). It has been said: al-witr with a fatha denotes number, and with a kasra denotes vengeance (al-dhahl). It has also been read "wa-l-watr" with a fatha on the waw and a kasra on the ta' (i.e., wa-l-watri).

Verse 4: "And by the night when it passes on." That is, it proceeds, as in His saying, exalted is He: "And by the night when it turns its back" (74:33), and "And by the night when it breathes away" (81:17). The restriction is due to what it contains of clear indication of perfect power and abundant blessing. Or [it means] "when it travels through it," from their saying "ṣallā al-maqām," i.e., it was prayed in it; the yā' is dropped being content with the kasra. It has been read with the yā' retained in general, and with it dropped only in pause specifically. It has also been read "yusrin" with tanwin, just as "wal-fajri" and "al-watri" have been read, and this is the tanwin that falls as a substitute for the vowel-lengthening letter of pause (ḥarf al-iṭlāq).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 89, verse 5:

﴿Is there in that an oath?﴾ ...etc. This is an affirmation and confirmation of the great dignity of the things sworn by, and that they are noble matters truly deserving of glorification and reverence in the eyes of people of intellect. It also alerts that swearing by them is a weighty matter, fitting for emphasizing a report, in the manner of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, it is an oath, if you only knew, a great one﴾ (56:76). "That" (dhalika) is a demonstrative referring either to the things sworn by (p-154)

by them, with the masculine form taking account of what was mentioned, as its verification has passed, or to the swearing by them. Whichever it is, the sense of distance in it serves to announce the elevated rank of what is pointed to and the remoteness of its station in nobility and excellence. That is: Is there in what has been mentioned of things an oath, i.e., a thing sworn by?

﴿for one of intellect (ḥijr)﴾: one who sees it as truly deserving to be sworn by, out of glorification and honor. The intended meaning is to confirm that the whole is so. This manner was chosen to belittle the creatures and to announce that the matter is evident. Or the meaning is: Is there, in My swearing by those things, an oath for one of intellect whose oath is accepted by him, who counts it significant, does likewise, and uses it to confirm the thing sworn to? The word ḥijr (intellect, i.e., the faculty that restrains its possessor from recklessness in what is not befitting) means reason, because it restrains its owner, that is, prevents him from rashness in what is unseemly. It is likewise called "reason" ('aql) and "restraint" (nuhya), because it comprehends and forbids; and also ḥaṣāh, from iḥṣā' which is control. Al-Farrā' said: It is said, "He is indeed one of ḥijr" when he is in command of himself and controls it. The thing sworn to is omitted, and it is "Surely he will be punished" (la-yu'adhdhabanna), as indicated by His saying, Exalted is He: *

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 89, verse 6:

﴿Have you not seen how your Lord dealt with ʿĀd?﴾ ... and so on. This is an appeal to the knowledge of the Prophet (ﷺ) by means of what points to the punishment of ʿĀd and their likes, who shared with his people (ﷺ) in transgression and corruption, following the manner of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Have you not seen the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord?﴾ (2:258), and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Have you not seen that they wander in every valley?﴾ (26:225). It is as if it were said: Do you not know with certain knowledge how your Lord punished ʿĀd and their counterparts, so He will punish these as well, since they share in what necessitates it of disbelief and sins? By "ʿĀd" is meant the descendants of ʿĀd ibn ʿAws ibn Iram ibn Sam ibn Noah (peace be upon him), the people of Hud (peace be upon him). They were named after their father, just as the Banu Hashim were named after Hashim. It has been said that their earlier generations were called ʿĀd al-Ula (the First ʿĀd) and their later generations ʿĀd al-Akhira (the Last ʿĀd). Imad al-Din ibn Kathir said: Every account in the Qur'an concerning ʿĀd refers to the First ʿĀd, except what is in Surat al-Ahqaf.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 89, verse 7:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Iram﴾ is an explicative apposition (ʿatf bayan) to "ʿAd," to indicate that they were the "first ʿAd," with an elided genitive construction, meaning: the lineage (sibt) of Iram, or the people (ahl) of Iram, according to what has been said, that Iram is the name of their city or their land in which they dwelt. The reading with the idafa (genitive construction) supports this. In any case, its being diptotic (imtina' sarfiha) is due to definiteness (ta'rif) and feminine gender (ta'nith). It has also been read as "Irm" with a sukun on the ra' for lightness, just as "bi-warqikum" was read.

﴿Dhat al-ʿImad﴾ is an adjective (sifa) of "Iram," meaning: possessing tall pillars (qudud tiwal), by likening their stature to pillars (a'mida). From this is the saying of the Arabs: "rajul ʿumud" and "ʿumudan," when a man is tall. Or it means: possessing tents and poles, since they were nomadic people of poles (ahl ʿumud). Or: possessing lofty buildings. Or: possessing columns (asatin), according to which Iram is the name of their city. It has been read as "Iram dhat al-ʿImad" with Iram in genitive construction with "dhat al-ʿImad." Al-Iram means a landmark (al-ʿilm), i.e., "ʿAd, the people of the landmarks of dhat al-ʿImad," according to which it is the name of their city. It has also been read as "Iram dhata al-ʿImad," meaning: God Most High made it into rubble (ramim). "Fa'ala Rabbuka" (your Lord did) is the substitute (badal) for it.

It has also been said: it is a supplicatory sentence (jumla du'a'iyya) interposed between the modified and the modifier. It is narrated that ʿAd had two sons, Shadid and Shaddad. They ruled and dominated, then Shadid died, and the matter passed entirely to Shaddad, who ruled the world, and its kings submitted to him. He heard the mention of Paradise and said: "I will build the like of it." So he built Iram in some of the deserts of Aden over three hundred years. It was a great city, its palaces of gold and silver, its columns of chrysolite and ruby, and in it were all kinds of trees and flowing rivers. When its building was completed, the people of his kingdom set out toward it. When they were at a distance of one day and night from it, God Most High sent upon them a cry (sayha) from the sky, and they perished.

And on the authority of ʿAbd Allah ibn Qilaba: he went out seeking his camels, came upon it, and carried away what he was able to of what was there. His report reached Muawiya, who summoned him and he related the matter to him. Muawiya sent to Kaʿb and asked him, and he said: "It is Iram dhat al-ʿImad, and a man of the Muslims will enter it in your time, ruddy, fair-haired, short, with a mole on his eyebrow and a mole on his heel, who will go out seeking his camels." Then he turned to Ibn Qilaba and said: "By God, this is that man."

The verse is "Which had not been created the like of in the lands" (﴿الَّتِي لَمْ يُخْلَقْ مِثْلُها في البِلادِ﴾). It is another attribute of "Iram" (Iram), meaning that no one like them was created in terms of the size of their bodies and their strength. The height of a man among them was four hundred cubits (dhira'), and he would come to a great rock, carry it, and throw it upon the tribe, destroying them. Or (it means): no city like the city of Shaddad (Shaddad) was created in all the lands of the world. It is also read as "lam yakhluq" (not created), with the verb attributed to Allah the Exalted.

And Thamud. [Thamud is] conjoined to "ʿAd." It is a well-known tribe, named after their forefather Thamud, brother of Jadis. The two were the sons of ʿAmir ibn Iram ibn Sam ibn Nuh, peace be upon him. They were Arabs of the ʿAribah (the original Arab tribes), who dwelt in al-Hijr between the Hijaz and Tabuk, and they worshipped idols as ʿAd did.

﴿who hewed out the rocks in the valley﴾ That is: they cut into the mountain rock and made for themselves dwellings hewn out of the stone, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you hew out houses from the mountains﴾. It is said they were the first to carve out mountains, rocks and marble, and they built seven hundred and one thousand cities, all of them of stone.

Translation:

﴿And Pharaoh, the possessor of stakes﴾ He was described thus because of the multitude of his soldiers and their tents, which they pitched (with stakes) at their encampments; or because of his torturing (people) with stakes.

﴿Who transgressed in the lands﴾ is either in the genitive case (majrur), as an attribute (sifah, a qualifying adjective) of those previously mentioned, or in the accusative (mansub) or nominative (marfu') case, by way of censure (dhamm). The meaning is: each group of them transgressed in their lands. The same applies to the discourse in His, the Exalted's, saying: *
﴿So they multiplied corruption therein﴾, that is: through disbelief and all sorts of disobedience.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 89, verse 13:

﴿Therefore your Lord poured down upon them﴾ i.e., He sent down a severe chastisement upon every group of those peoples, immediately after what they had done of transgression and corruption.

﴿a scourge of punishment﴾ i.e., a severe punishment whose extent cannot be fully grasped. It is an expression for the various kinds of punishment that befell each of them, which were explained in the other noble surahs. Calling it a "scourge" points to the fact that, compared with what has been prepared for them in the Hereafter, it is like the whip beside the sword. The expression of its descent as "pouring" (ṣabb) indicates its abundance, continuity and succession, for it is a figure for the spilling of a fluid or something that flows like it, such as sand or grains, and its emptying out with intensity, abundance and continuity. Its attribution to the whip, although it is not of that kind, is by way of likening its successive descent, overtaking the one struck, to the drops of a poured liquid.

It has been said: the "sawt" (scourge, or mixture) is: (p-156)

the mixing of one thing with another. The meaning then is: what was mixed for them of kinds of punishment. It has also been explained as "portion" (naṣīb) and as "severity" (shiddah), since the word sawt is applied to each of these in the lexicon. Therefore there is no need, on this reading, to consider the repeated attachment of the whip to the one being punished in order to liken it to something poured, as in the first meaning. Each of these meanings is by itself capable of continuity.

And His, may He be exalted, saying:

The Almighty's saying: ﴿Indeed your Lord is ever watchful﴾ is a causal explanation of what precedes it, and an announcement that the disbelievers of his people, upon him be blessings and peace, will be struck by a punishment like that which befell those mentioned, as is indicated by the mention of the title of Lordship (rububiyya) together with its attribution to his pronoun, upon him be blessings and peace. It has also been said that it is the response to the oath, and what lies between them is a parenthetical interjection. Al-mirsad (the place of watching) is the place where one awaits observation; it is on the pattern of mif'al from rasadahu, like al-miqat from waqtahu. This is an image of His, the Exalted's, watching over the disobedient, and that they cannot escape Him.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 89, verse 15:

His statement, the Exalted, ﴿As for man﴾ ... etc., is connected to what precedes it, as if it were said: He, the Exalted, is intent on observing the conditions of His servants and recompensing them for their deeds, good and evil. As for man, that does not concern him; rather, the aim of his gaze and the focus of his thoughts is this world and its pleasures.

﴿When his Lord tests him﴾, i.e., treats him as one who tests him with wealth and ease. The fa' in His statement, the Exalted, ﴿then He honours him and bestows favours upon him﴾ is explanatory (tafsiriyyah), for honouring and bestowing favours are part of the testing.

﴿Then he says, "My Lord has honoured me"﴾, i.e., He has favoured me with what He has given me of wealth and standing, as I deserve. It does not occur to him that it is a bounty bestowed upon him in order to test him, whether he will be grateful or ungrateful. This is the predicate (khabar) of the subject (mubtada'), which is man (al-insan). The fa' is due to the meaning of the conditional (shart) contained in "amma" (as for). The intervening adverbial phrase (zarf) is in the intention of postponement, as if it were said: "As for man, he says, 'My Lord has honoured me,' at the time of his being tested with blessings." Its placement at the front is to indicate from the outset that the honouring and bestowing of favours occur by way of testing, so that the corruption of his stated claim may become clear.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 89, verse 16:

﴿And as for him, when his Lord tests him⁠﴾, i.e., and as for him, when his Lord tests him.

﴿and restricts his provision for him⁠﴾, according as His will requires, which is founded upon far-reaching wisdoms.

﴿then he says: "My Lord has humiliated me⁠﴾. It does not occur to him that this is a trial to see whether he will be patient or impatient, although it is not in any way humiliation at all; rather, restriction may lead to honor in both abodes, and expansion may lead to the loss of both. It is also read "fa-qaddara" with the shadda (intensive form), and it is read "akramani" and "ahanani" with the ya' (of the first person) affirmed, and "akraman" and "ahanan" with the nun sukun in pause.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 89, verse 17:

﴿Kallā﴾ is a rebuke (radʿ) to man concerning his stated claim, and a denial of it in both of its states. Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him) said: The meaning is: "I did not test him with wealth because of his honour before Me, nor did I test him with poverty because of his humiliation before Me; rather, that is purely by way of qadaʾ and qadar (divine decree and predestination)." Carrying the rebuke and denial over to his last statement is far-fetched.

As for His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿Nay, but you do not honour the orphan﴾, this is a transition from explaining his bad sayings to explaining his bad deeds. The turn to direct address (al-iltifāt ilā al-khiṭāb) signals that his earlier offence requires being noticed by confronting him with the reproach, to intensify the censure and emphasise the condemnation. The plural is used with regard to the meaning of man (al-insān), since what is intended is the category (al-jins), i.e.: "Nay, but you have states that are worse in evil than what has been mentioned, and more indicative of your greed for wealth, in that Allah honours you with an abundance of wealth, yet you do not fulfil what is obligatory upon you concerning it, namely honouring the orphan by showing him kindness." It has also been read as "lā yukrimūn" (they do not honour).

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 89, verse 18:**

﴿And do not urge one another﴾ with the deletion of one of the two tā's from tatahāddūn (meaning: none of you urges another).

﴿upon the feeding of the poor﴾ That is, upon feeding him. It is also read "tahāddūn" (from al-muhāddah, mutual urging), and it is read "yahuddūn" with the yā' and with the tā'.

Qur'anic quotation: ﴿And you devour the heritage﴾ means: the inheritance, and its root is "wurath."

﴿Devouring greedily (aklan lamman)﴾ means: having lamm, that is, combining what is lawful and what is unlawful (lamm: gathering together, mixing), for they did not give inheritance to women and children, and they would consume their shares; or they would consume what the deceased had gathered from both lawful and unlawful means, knowing this.
﴿And you love wealth with an intense love﴾, much, together with eagerness and avarice. It is also recited as "يُحِبُّونَ" (yuḥibbūna) with a yāʾ (ياء), that is, in the third person, "they love."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 89, verse 21:

﴿Kalla﴾ is a rebuke to them concerning that. The words of the Exalted, ﴿When the earth is crushed, crushed to pieces﴾ ... etc., form a resumptive statement (isti'naf) brought in the manner of a warning, as a justification (ta'lil) for the rebuke. That is: when the earth is crushed, crushed continuously, until it is broken and all that is on its surface of mountains, buildings and palaces is gone, at the time it is shaken and becomes scattered dust (habaan munbaththan). It is also said: al-dakk (crushing) is the leveling of what is raised by spreading out and smoothing, so the meaning is: when it is levelled, levelling after levelling, and nothing remains on its surface, until it becomes like a smooth rock. Whichever of these is meant, it is an expression of what befalls it at the second blast (al-nafkhah al-thaniyah).

**﴿And your Lord comes﴾**, meaning: the signs of His power and the effects of His dominion become manifest, in the manner that appears when a sovereign is present, through the rulings of his awe and governance. It was also said: His command and His decree come, with an omitted noun (ḥadhf al-muḍāf) for the sake of magnifying the matter (li-l-tahwīl).

**﴿And the angels, rank upon rank﴾**, meaning: arranged in rows, or possessors of ranks. For on that Day the angels of every heaven will descend, and they will stand in rows, one row after another, according to their stations and levels, encircling the jinn and humankind.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 89, verse 23:

﴿And on that Day Hell will be brought forth﴾, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and Hellfire will be made manifest﴾. Ibn Mas'ud and Muqatil said: Hell will be led along by seventy thousand chains, each chain held by seventy thousand angels who drag it until it is set up on the left of the Throne, and it has rage and roaring. Muslim has narrated this in his Sahih from Ibn Mas'ud, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

﴿On that Day﴾ is a *badal* (substitution, i.e. an apposition that replaces the earlier noun) for "when the earth is leveled", and the governing element (*'amil*) of both is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿man will remember﴾. That is, he will remember what he neglected, in its details, by witnessing its effects and its rulings, or by seeing it with his own eyes, on the basis that deeds take on bodily form in the next life, so that each of the good and bad deeds appears in forms suited to it, the beautiful forms or the ugly ones (p-158) or he will be admonished. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and how can remembrance be for him?﴾ is an *i'tiraD* (parenthetical interjection) inserted to establish that he does not truly remember, since his remembrance is void of benefit because it does not occur at its proper time. The word *anna* ("how") is the predicate placed first (*khabar muqaddam*), *al-dhikra* ("remembrance") is the subject (*mubtada'*), and *lahu* ("for him") is connected to what the predicate is connected to. That is: and from where can remembrance be his, when its time has passed? It has been said that there is an omitted modifier here, meaning: and how can the benefit of remembrance be for him, and using this to argue that accepting repentance is not obligatory in the abode of obligation is baseless, since his remembrance is not repentance at all, for he knows that repentance can only occur in this world, as His saying, exalted is He, indicates: *

﴿He says, "Would that I had sent forward for my life!"﴾ This is a *badal ishtimal* (an inclusive apposition, in which the second term includes or pertains to the first) of "yatadhakkaru" (he remembers), or it is a *isti'naf* (a resumed new sentence), coming as an answer to a question that arises from it, as though it were said: "What does he say when he remembers?" So it was said: "He says: Would that I had done good works for this life of mine, or during my life in this world, which I could benefit from today."

There is no indication in this wish that the servant independently originates his act. What it indicates is the belief that he was able to send forward good works. As for whether that ability is by the sheer power of the servant or by God's creation at the moment He directs the servant's acquisitive power (*qudrah kasibah*, the power by which one acquires an act) toward it, the answer is "no" to the former. As for what has been said, that one who is prevented (from acting) may still wish if it were possible for him, this may give the impression that whoever directs his power toward one of the two sides of an action believes himself prevented from the other side. That is not so. Rather, everyone is certain that if he directed his power toward whichever side of his voluntary actions he chose, it would be achieved. On this rests the orbit of moral obligation (*taklif*) and the establishing of proof.

﴿So on that Day﴾, i.e., the Day when what has been mentioned of states and words will take place.

﴿None will punish as He punishes﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 89, verse 26:

﴿And none will bind as He binds.﴾ The pronoun in "وِثاقَهُ" (wathaqahu, "His binding") refers to God the Exalted. That is: none other than Him takes charge of God's punishment and His binding, since the whole matter belongs to Him. Or the pronoun refers to the human being, meaning: none of the zabaniyah (the angels of punishment, lit. "the pushers") punishes as they punish him. The two verbs have also been read in the passive voice (yu'adhdhabu and yuwthaqu), with the pronoun still referring to the human being. It has also been said that the intended person is Ubayy ibn Khalaf, meaning: no one punishes with a punishment like his, and no one binds with chains and shackles like his binding, because of his extreme disbelief and obstinacy. It has also been said: no one bears the punishment of the human being, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾.

The Most High's words, ﴿O tranquil soul﴾, are a description of the state of one who finds rest in the remembrance of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and in obeying Him, following the description of the state of one who finds rest in this world. It is described as "tranquil" (al-iṭmi'nān) because it ascends through the stages of causes and effects to the Originator who acts by His own essence. It therefore comes to rest in knowing Him, and in its existence and all its affairs it becomes entirely independent of anything else through Him. It has also been said: it is the soul at rest in the truth, which has reached the coolness of certainty, such that no doubt whatsoever stirs within it. It has also been said: it is the soul that is secure, which fear and grief do not unsettle. This is supported by the reading: "O soul that is secure and tranquil" (p-159)

Allah, the Most High, says this Himself directly, just as He spoke to Moses (peace be upon him), or through the tongue of an angel at the completion of the reckoning of people. This is the most apparent view. It has also been said that it is said at the Resurrection, and it has been said that it is said at death.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 89, verse 28:

﴿Return to your Lord﴾, i.e., to His promise or to His command.

﴿Well-pleased﴾ with what you have been given of everlasting bliss, ﴿and well-pleasing﴾ in the sight of Allah, Mighty and Majestic,
"So enter among My servants" — into the company of My servants, the righteous ones specially devoted to Me.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 89, verse 30:

﴿Enter My Paradise﴾ along with them, or join the row of those brought near (al-muqarrabun) and be illuminated by their lights, for the holy essences (al-jawahir al-qudsiyyah) are like mirrors facing one another. It was also said that the intended meaning of "the soul" (al-nafs) is the spirit (al-ruh), and the meaning is: enter the bodies of My servants from which you departed, and enter the abode of My reward. This supports the view that the address takes place at the Resurrection (al-ba'th). It was read as "fa-udkhuli fi 'ibadi" (enter among My servants), and read as "fi jasad 'abdi" (into the body of My servant). It was also said that it was revealed concerning Hamzah ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, and it was said that it was revealed concerning Habib ibn 'Adi, may Allah be pleased with them both. The apparent meaning is generality.

From the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surat al-Fajr on the ten nights, he will be forgiven; and whoever recites it on the rest of the days, it will be a light for him on the Day of Resurrection."
